Terminal Fog

The fog takes the city apart and puts it back almost right.

The Repair People patch the city all day, one wall at a time. Some things cannot be patched. For those, Terminal City has the fog. Late at night, after the rooms have emptied and the Freight has taken away what cannot stay, fog comes in from the water and covers the shoreline, the tracks, the lights, the skyline, until enough of Vancouver is hidden for Terminal City to be rebuilt underneath. This is the full rebuild, the one that fixes what a brush cannot. When the fog lifts the city is back. Almost. One familiar thing is gone, or shifted, or slightly wrong, and nobody announces it. **Continuity.** After 19; final chapter in continuous story order. Repeat established courtyard compositions so the small change is visible. Closing Meeting is a short return, not a twentieth chapter.

After the Freight, fog comes in from the water. It covers the rails first, then the warehouse lights, then the upper windows of the new development. The painter carries the recovered bucket down the lane beyond the crossing and disappears into the fog.

Repair People can work a wall at a time. Terminal Fog works while the walls cannot be seen. It hides enough of Vancouver for the things that local repairs could not settle to be put back together. No one gets to watch the middle of the job.

Before dawn, the courtyard returns in pieces: entrance, window, branch, bench. At the rear, the sealed doorway looks almost right. Yesterday its shadow crossed a brick joint. This morning the joint lies just beyond the shadow. The bricks are still bricks; the door is still closed.

On the pale wall, the residents' crooked marks remain. The unpainted gap remains too. Someone brings a cup downstairs and sits before opening a phone. The upstairs window opens, and music reaches the bench.

The painter passes the entrance on the way to Trout Lake. For a moment the bucket stops swinging. The painter looks at the crooked stroke, then at the person sitting beneath it. The bucket begins to swing again.

At the lake, crows are already gathering. The others arrive by their separate routes. Somewhere else in Vancouver there is another wall, another window, another place worth stopping. The painter sits down and opens a hand.

The ruleEverything has returned so far.

Terminal City · Storybook v0.9.0 · built 2026-09-12
Terminal City is an original fictional mythology inspired by Vancouver’s geography, weather, wildlife, infrastructure, art, and electronic music. It makes no claim to historical, Indigenous, or religious tradition. Real places are used as settings; the operating system layered on them is invented.
Made by Steve Hiehn, a software developer and electronic musician based in Vancouver, Canada. All music was created using a custom DAW, Signals & Sorcery.
